6169_ask_me_dont_tell_me_E00754_01_23_24.sy: In San Francisco, the work of the Youth for Service Program, founded by Carl May, is presented. The Program's core mission is to reduce juvenile delinquency, the means to do so by giving at risk youth, regardless of ethnicity or background including criminal, a purpose in doing volunteer work, largely for the less able in the community such as the disabled and/or the elderly, the Program ultimately directed by them and not by "authority". The work itself is not judged, and the Program is not designed as a skills training one, although the participants can learn some valuable skills for future employment. While giving the boys a sense of accomplishment, the Program also provide rewards and perks as further incentives. The Program is meant to give the youth a sense of acceptance while giving the community as a whole a sense of trust. May started the Program targeting what are known as the "jacketed" gangs, the most visible of the juveniles for which the program is aimed. Out of the Program, the youths themselves have formed a council to give themselves a say on those issues that are important to them, and a forum for themselves to work out whatever differences they may have internally.

calling-the-tune.sy: Calling the Tune offers a fascinating look at the fledgeling gramophone industry as it tries to solve the problems of reliable recording and production methods. 'I predict that the gramophone will be the democratic entertainment of the future' states unscrupulous record label boss Mr Gordon (Sam Livesey), who finally gets his comeuppance after one dirty trick too far against his rivals. If the film's love story is perfunctory, the real interest comes with watching performers of the day, from Henry Wood and his orchestra to George Robey and Charles 'the laughing policeman' Penrose laying down their recordings direct to record. silent-a-sporting-chance.sy: The clerks at a New York hotel near Times Square turn away customers until they approve millionaire John Stonehouse and give him room 420. While attempting suicide, John hears a shot from a nearby room. Finding Gilberte Bonheur bending over the limp body of Aaron Witt, whom, she says, she shot when he tried to assault her, John, wanting to die anyway, offers to take the blame. He escapes after recovering an emerald that Witt used to blackmail Gilberte. After Gilberte, Witt, and the clerks conspire, John helps Gilberte hide Witt, who revives and demands the emerald or its value. John writes a check and leaves taking a theater ticket given to him by Gilbert. Cured, he goes to the theater and sees the happenings in the hotel enacted. Backstage, Gilberte explains that the ruse was to prove to a critic that the plot could really happen. the-phantom-of-the-opera-1930-sound-re-i.sy: The re-release of "The Phantom of the Opera" on February 16th, 1930, marked a significant moment in the film's history, as it coincided with the transition from silent films to "talkies," or films with synchronized sound. Originally released in 1925 as a silent film directed by Rupert Julian and starring Lon Chaney, the 1930 re-release aimed to update the movie for audiences experiencing the advent of sound cinema. During this re-release, the film underwent several modifications to incorporate sound elements, capitalize on the popularity of talking pictures, and attract new audiences. Some of the key changes and enhancements introduced during the 1930 re-release include: Addition of Sound Sequences: Sound sequences, including synchronized sound effects, dialogue, and music, were added to certain scenes throughout the film. the-wind_1928.sy: The Wind is a 1928 American synchronized sound romantic drama film directed by Victor Sjöström. While the film has no audible dialog, it was released with a synchronized musical score with sound effects using both the sound-on-disc and sound-on-film process. The movie was adapted by Frances Marion from the 1925 novel of the same name written by Dorothy Scarborough. Featuring Lillian Gish, Lars Hanson and Montagu Love, it is one of the last films released by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer without audible dialogue and is considered to be among the greatest "silent" films.
